commands.description: Lists every process and network socket grouped by app, with listening ports and signing state. This is also what plain `monitor-lizard` prints.
commands.title: Print the grouped snapshot

commands.description: Lists launch agents, launch daemons and cron jobs. Items not seen before are marked NEW.
commands.title: List startup items

commands.description: Prints one CPU, memory, network, disk and GPU sample as JSON.
commands.title: Print one metrics sample

commands.description: Scans a fixed list of known folders (developer caches, app caches, logs, Downloads, Mail, Applications and node_modules folders) and prints their sizes on disk as JSON, each labelled safe, review or yours, with how much of the disk is used, purgeable and open. It only reads, stops after 20 seconds and runs at low priority.
commands.title: Show where space went

commands.description: Prints the trust label, the rules that fired and the actions allowed for one app group.
commands.title: Explain why a group got its label

commands.description: Sends the evidence for one group to a model server on this Mac (default port 8090) and prints its reply. Nothing leaves the machine.
commands.title: Ask a local model about a group

commands.description: Prints each sudo or su run, with the chain of parent processes, until you press Ctrl-C. Each event is also saved to the history database.
commands.title: Watch for sudo and su
commands.undo: Quit and delete ~/.monitor-lizard/history.db to drop the saved events.

commands.description: Prints the last n (default 20) events saved by `watch`.
commands.title: Show recent sudo and su events

commands.description: Prints authorization attempts from the last n minutes (default 60), including failures and the parent process.
commands.title: Show recent privilege prompts

commands.description: Prints the same data the dashboard loads, for scripts and agents.
commands.title: Print the full snapshot as JSON

commands.description: Serves the dashboard on 127.0.0.1 (default port 4747). The dashboard can stop your own processes after you confirm, and saves history to ~/.monitor-lizard/.
commands.title: Start the dashboard
commands.undo: Press Ctrl-C to stop the server. A stopped process cannot be restarted from the dashboard.

commands.description: `install` prints the pinned repo, commit, size and licence, then with --yes downloads that one file from Hugging Face, verifies its SHA-256 and refuses anything else. `status` reads and hashes the local file only, without contacting Hugging Face.
commands.title: Download and verify the local model

commands.description: The agent's kill switch, off by default. On: the Apps drawer shows the suggestion, and a running `serve` starts supervising llama-server (loopback only, cleared environment) once the model is installed and memory pressure allows it, and `/api/classify` can get a model-backed verdict. Shadow: the same, and every verdict is recorded in the history for 14 days, but the dashboard shows nothing. Off: any running llama-server stops, and every classification is the rule label alone. `agent verdicts [count]` prints the recorded verdicts, newest first.
commands.title: Turn the local agent on or off
commands.undo: Run `monitor-lizard agent off` (or `on` or `shadow`, to undo turning it off).

commands.description: Adds each item to the baseline of expected things, so it is no longer reported as new. A key is an app group key, or app:<key>, host:<app key>|<address>, startup:<plist path>#<fingerprint> (as the dashboard sends it; a startup entry that is only the path matches any version of that item, and exists only if you wrote it by hand) or finding:<app key>:<rule>#<ports>.
commands.title: Mark items as expected
commands.undo: Press Unmark on the item in the dashboard, or remove its entry from baseline.json in ~/.monitor-lizard/.

commands.description: Prints the commands and terms whose title, command or tags contain the word. With no word it prints all of them.
commands.title: Search this guide

commands.description: Shows size, used and available space of the startup volume. Used can look small because macOS counts the other volumes in the same container separately.

example.output:
Filesystem        Size    Used   Avail Capacity iused ifree %iused  Mounted on
/dev/disk3s1s1   460Gi    13Gi    36Gi    27%    484k  374M    0%   /

commands.title: Free space on the startup disk

commands.description: Lists each APFS container with the space its volumes use and how much is not allocated, then every volume with its role and size.

example.output:
APFS Containers (6 found)
|
+-- Container disk3 <uuid>
|   ====================================================
|   APFS Container Reference:     disk3
|   Size (Capacity Ceiling):      494384795648 B (494.4 GB)
|   Capacity In Use By Volumes:   456152682496 B (456.2 GB) (92.3% used)
|   Capacity Not Allocated:       38232113152 B (38.2 GB) (7.7% free)

commands.title: APFS containers and volumes

commands.description: Lists the dates of local snapshots on the startup volume. It shows dates only, not sizes.
commands.title: List local Time Machine snapshots

commands.description: Deletes every local Time Machine snapshot with that date (format YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS, as listed above) on all mounted disks. The man page does not say it needs root; the usual instruction is to run it with sudo and to give the terminal Full Disk Access. Labelled needs sudo as the safe assumption.
commands.title: Delete one local snapshot
commands.undo: None. The snapshot is gone; Time Machine makes a new one at its next run.

commands.description: Sums each folder in your Library and sorts them smallest to largest. It can take a minute on a large Library. The example shortens the absolute paths that `du` prints to `~`.
commands.title: Largest folders in your Library

commands.description: Deletes simulator devices that the installed Xcode no longer supports, and their data.
commands.title: Delete unusable Xcode simulators
commands.undo: None. Create new simulators in Xcode if you need them again.

commands.description: Shows the space used by images, containers, local volumes and build cache. It needs the Docker daemon to be running.
commands.title: Docker disk use

commands.description: Asks for confirmation, then removes stopped containers, networks no container uses, dangling images and dangling build cache. `--all` also removes every unused image, `--volumes` also removes anonymous volumes, and `-f` skips the question.
commands.title: Remove unused Docker data
commands.undo: None. Images can be pulled or rebuilt again; files in removed containers and anonymous volumes are lost.

commands.description: Lists the old versions and cached downloads that `brew cleanup` would remove, and how much space that frees. The -n flag removes nothing.

example.output:
Would remove: /opt/homebrew/Library/Homebrew/vendor/portable-ruby/<version> (1,707 files, 34.6MB)
==> This operation would free approximately 69.3MB of disk space.

commands.title: Preview Homebrew clean-up

terms.meaning: Apple File System, the format of the startup disk. Volumes in one container share its free space, so each volume's size changes as the others grow.
A copy of the disk's state that Time Machine keeps on the Mac. macOS removes it when space runs low.
Space held by caches and snapshots that macOS frees on demand. It counts as available in Finder and as used in `df`.
The Storage settings category for everything that is not an app, document or media file: caches, logs, snapshots and developer files.
A privacy permission an app needs before it can read protected folders such as Mail and Messages.
A property-list file that starts a program when you log in. Launch daemons do the same at boot, with system rights.
A process waiting for incoming network connections on a port. A star marks one reachable from other machines.
All processes and sockets that belong to one app, shown as one row.
The verdict a rule gives a group, such as yours, Apple or unknown. Rules set it, never a model.
